prompt:
# Write one behaviour-tree node that ADJUSTS an existing navigator

You are writing a single node for the behaviour tree of a Unitree Go2 quadruped
navigating an indoor space it has no map of.

Below the node is an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy. The
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`. You never
touch the policy, the gait, or the joints.

**You are not writing the navigator.** A navigator already exists, it already
drives, and it will keep driving whether or not your node does anything. Your
node sits above it and revises what it asked for.

Return **one Python module**, in one fenced ```python block, and nothing else
that looks like code. Everything you want to say in prose, say outside the
fence. What the module must contain is set out in "What to return" at the end.

## How the tree runs: a layered command pipeline

Every node in the tree ticks, **every step, in order**. Nothing short-circuits
anything.

    Layer[ ports, BASE, node_1, node_2, ... ]
             ^      ^      ^
             |      |      `- each may revise the fields it declared
             |      `-------- proposes a whole command, every tick
             `--------------- publishes a few facts from the sensors

The **base** is a general indoor navigator. It gets the robot most of the way
most of the time, it handles the awkward cases, and it never declines to act.
Each later node may then adjust individual fields of what the base proposed.

This is subsumption: a competent low layer, refined by narrow higher ones. Your
node is one of the higher ones.

**So the thing you are writing is small.** It does one thing to one part of the
command, under one condition, and the rest of the time it stays out of the way.

## The one hard rule: you declare which fields you may write

Your class declares `WRITES` — the Twist fields it is allowed to touch:

```python
WRITES = ("vx",)            # may bound or set forward speed, nothing else
WRITES = ("wz",)            # may steer, but may not change speed
WRITES = ("vx", "wz")       # both. Only if the mechanism genuinely needs both.
```

This is **enforced, not advisory.** Writing a field you did not declare raises
immediately and the node is rejected. Declare the smallest set your mechanism
actually needs — a node that declares all three is claiming to be a navigator,
and it will be judged as one.

Two ways to write, and they are the only two:

```python
ports.cap(vx=0.35)       # min(|pending|, 0.35), sign kept. Never speeds up.
ports.adjust(wz=0.8)     # replaces the field outright. Last writer wins.
```

Prefer `cap` whenever the mechanism is a limit, a bound, or a "no faster than"
— it composes with other caps in any order, which `adjust` does not.

And you can see what the base asked for:

```python
pending = ports.command          # a Command(vx, vy, wz). Never None when you
                                 # tick, because the base ticks before you.
if pending.vx > my_limit:
    ports.cap(vx=my_limit)
```

**Do not call `ports.drive(...)`.** That writes the whole command and is the
base's job; it raises for a node that narrowed `WRITES`.

## Declining is a first-class outcome, and it is free

Return `Status.FAILURE` from `precondition`, or simply write nothing in `tick`,
and the base's command passes through **byte-identical**. The robot behaves
exactly as if your node were not in the tree.

That matters more than it sounds. Your node's contribution is measured by adding
it to the tree and re-running the same worlds: it can only be credited for the
episodes it changes, and it is blamed for every episode it breaks. A node that
acts only when its trigger genuinely holds is a good node. A node that fires on
every tick has replaced the base rather than supported it, and it will be
measured as having done so.

## The node contract

A leaf is one of three kinds, and the kind is the class you subclass:

- **`Condition`** — answers one question about the world and publishes it as a
  port. Never touches the Twist.
- **`Action`** — the only kind that may touch the Twist. With a narrowed
  `WRITES` it is a *modifier*, which is what you are writing.
- **`Decorator`** — wraps exactly one child and governs whether the child runs.
  Never touches the Twist itself.

Your class declares, as class attributes:

| Attribute | What it is |
|---|---|
| `WRITES` | the Twist fields this node may write. See above. |
| `PORTS` | a tuple of `Port` — the typed interface between nodes. See below. |
| `PRECONDITION` | one sentence: when this node applies |
| `EFFECT` | one sentence: what this node changes |
| `TAGS` | a tuple of short strings, for retrieval |

and implements:

```python
def reset(self, scenario, rng):    # clear per-episode state. optional.
def precondition(self, obs, ports) -> bool:   # default: always True
def tick(self, obs, ports) -> Status:         # Status.SUCCESS / FAILURE / RUNNING
```

**One precondition and one effect.** A node that needs two of either is two
nodes. This is not a style rule: contribution is measured by adding one node at
a time, and a node with two effects is attributable to neither.

**No coupling to a specific scenario.** Your node will be run on procedurally
generated worlds you have never seen. It may not name a room, a coordinate, a
doorway or a map. Anything it knows about the world it learns through `obs` at
tick time.

### Ports

Ports are how nodes pass information to each other. They are **not** a
blackboard: at tick time you are handed a `PortView` restricted to exactly the
ports you declared, and touching anything else raises immediately.

```python
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.IN)    # you read it:   value = ports["name"]
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.OUT)   # you write it:  ports["name"] = value
```

The port vocabulary is **closed**. These seven types and no others:

| `PortType` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `POSE` | `(x, y, yaw)` — a belief about where the robot is, never ground truth |
| `BEARING` | radians, robot frame unless the port name says otherwise |
| `SPEED` | m/s, non-negative |
| `RANGES` | an array of beam returns, metres |
| `CONFIDENCE` | `[0, 1]` — how much to trust something |
| `FLAG` | a boolean fact about the episode |
| `REGION` | an area of the floor, `(x, y, radius)` |

Three ports are always published before your node ticks, so you may declare any
of them as inputs: `goal_known` (FLAG), `pose` (POSE), `ranges` (RANGES).
Anything else you declare as an input must be published by another node earlier
in the Layer, and if nothing does, the tree refuses to build.

Publish an OUT port when the quantity you computed is genuinely useful to
someone else — a limit, a bearing, a confidence. Do not publish your own
internal state.

### What to import

Exactly these, and nothing else.

```python
import math
import numpy as np

from core.observation import Command
from nodes.contract import (Action, Condition, Decorator, Direction, Port,
                            PortType, Status)
```

Import only what you use. You will usually not need `Command` at all: a modifier
revises fields, it does not construct commands.

### What your node can see

`tick` is handed an `Observation`, frozen, one per control step:

```python
obs.t                   # sim seconds since the episode started
obs.ranges              # np.ndarray, 181 beams, metres, inf where no return
obs.range_angles        # np.ndarray, beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
obs.range_max           # 6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
obs.pose_estimate       # (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, not the truth
obs.pose_error_estimate # scalar, metres — how wrong we think the belief is
obs.contact             # bool — are we touching something right now
obs.goal                # (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of these are traps and both are deliberate:

- **`pose_estimate` is a belief.** On some scenarios a seeded random walk is
  added to it and it drifts away from the truth. Ground truth is never in
  `Observation`; the runner keeps it for scoring only.
- **`obs.goal` may be `None`**, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still
  scored against it, but this robot has not found it yet. It **latches**: once
  disclosed it stays disclosed. Your node runs on scenarios that withhold the
  goal and on scenarios that do not, so **handle `None` explicitly**. Do not
  assume a tuple.

The scan is 181 beams over a full circle, so `obs.ranges[0]` is not the front —
find the beam you want through `obs.range_angles`.

Speeds are saturated by the runner to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and
`|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Asking for more is not an error; it is just clipped.

## The task family this node has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is known, in an indoor space with no map. Walls and furniture occlude; the route is not a straight line and the obstruction is often not visible until the robot is close to it.

## What to base the node on

A principle card has been written for this task. **Implement this principle and
nothing else.**

```yaml
id: pi_terminal_spiral_search
node_name: SpiralSearchAtBelievedGoal

mechanism: A dead-reckoned position estimate degrades monotonically along a journey, because each increment of motion is added onto the previous estimate and each increment carries error. The paper's consequence is that the integrator is accurate enough to steer a long approach but NOT accurate enough to terminate one: "in conditions in which navigation has to be very precise, such as during the final approach to a goal, PI is too error-prone to be wholly relied upon" (p. 186). Animals that rely on path integration therefore do not stop when the integrator reads zero. They change behavioural mode: hamsters and desert ants both "switch from a fairly linear homeward progression to circular movements" once the integrator indicates proximity to the goal (p. 186), sweeping the neighbourhood of the believed goal instead of trusting the believed goal. The mode switch converts an unbounded point-accuracy requirement into a bounded area-coverage requirement: the straight leg only has to deliver the animal to within the search radius, and the search does the rest. This helps precisely when the integrator is wrong, and costs distance when it is right.

trigger: goal is not None, AND the residual goal vector computed in the belief frame, d = || goal - (pose_estimate.x, pose_estimate.y) ||, has fallen to or below the switch radius r_switch (defined in derivation), AND this leaf has not already spent its per-episode budget. The leaf yields (returns RUNNING to the parent's higher-priority avoidance branch, resuming afterwards from its stored spiral phase) whenever contact is True or the minimum range within +/-30 deg of the current heading is below 0.4 m; obstacle handling is not part of this mechanism and belongs to another node.

derivation: MAPPING (paper -> this robot). The animal's path integrator maps onto `pose_estimate`: both are recursive self-motion estimates, never observable against ground truth, and both accumulate error without bound - the scenario's seeded random walk added to `pose_estimate` is a literal instantiation of the paper's "necessarily cumulative" errors (p. 184). The animal's stored nest-to-food vector maps onto `goal`, and the paper's homing rule - subtract "the (short-term) nest-to-current-position vector from the (long-term) nest-to-food-site vector, up to zero vector" (p. 185) - is exactly `goal - pose_estimate[:2]`. "Circular movements ... near the nest entrance" maps onto a planar Archimedean spiral driven through the Twist interface, since the frozen locomotion policy accepts nothing else. WHERE THE MAPPING IS MINE, NOT THE PAPER'S. (1) The animals terminate their search by recognising familiar cues at the nest entrance. This robot has no goal detector of any kind - a planar lidar cannot recognise a goal - so the search is run open-loop and arrival is adjudicated by the scorer, not by the robot. This is the one place the biology does not carry over, and I am substituting a radius-and-timeout termination for cue recognition. (2) `pose_error_estimate` has no counterpart in the paper: the animal does not read out its own integrator error. Using it to size the search is my construction. (3) The paper states no spiral pitch, no switch radius and no search duration. Every number below is mine. NUMBERS. Switch radius r_switch = clip(1.5 * pose_error_estimate, 0.7, 3.0) metres. The 1.5 factor covers the tail of a zero-mean drift of scale `pose_error_estimate`, so the true goal lies inside the swept disc for the large majority of seeds. The 0.7 m floor is one Go2 body length, below which a spiral is not physically meaningful; the 3.0 m ceiling is half `range_max`, so the search stays inside sensed space. Spiral: r(phi) = r0 + b*phi/(2*pi), with r0 = 0.35 m and pitch b = 0.5 m per turn, phi accumulated in radians of arc about the believed goal. r0 = 0.35 m is forced by the actuator envelope, not chosen: a circle of radius r at speed v needs wz = v/r, and at the chosen v = 0.35 m/s the |wz| <= 1.0 rad/s limit gives r >= 0.35 m exactly. v = 0.35 m/s (well under the 0.8 m/s cap) leaves headroom for the avoidance branch to preempt. Pitch 0.5 m means successive turns are 0.5 m apart, so any success radius >= 0.25 m is swept with no gap - I do not know the scorer's success radius, and 0.25 m is my assumption about it. Command law each step: with e = goal - pose_estimate[:2] and the spiral centre fixed at that believed goal, drive vx = 0.35, vy = 0.0, wz = clip(0.35 / r(phi), -1.0, 1.0), advancing phi by (vx/r(phi)) * dt. Exit and hand control back to the goal-seeking leaf when r(phi) >= r_switch, or after 60 s of accumulated spiral time - at 0.35 m/s and pitch 0.5 m, covering a disc of radius 3.0 m costs about pi*3.0^2/0.5 = 57 m of path, so a budget is needed; 60 s buys about 21 m, i.e. full coverage out to ~1.8 m.

prediction:
  statement: On scenarios where pose_estimate drifts, a controller that spirals outward around the believed goal instead of halting at it reaches the true goal on a strictly larger fraction of seeds than one that drives the residual goal vector to zero and stops.
  metric: goal_reached
  baseline: goal_seeker
  min_effect: 0.1
  cost_metric: path_length
```

The fields mean what they say, and each one has a job:

- **mechanism** — what happens, and why it helps. This is the node body.
- **trigger** — when it applies. This is the precondition, and under the layered
  pipeline it is doing real work: outside the trigger your node must leave the
  base's command alone.
- **derivation** — how the principle becomes a rule for a Go2 with a 181-beam 2D
  scan. Where the derivation and your instincts disagree, follow the derivation:
  it is what the card is for.
- **prediction** — the falsifiable claim. **Restate it verbatim** in
  `PREDICTION`: the metric, the baseline and the minimum effect are the card's,
  not yours.
- **node_name** — what the leaf is called. Use it as the class name.

You are not told where this principle came from, and you do not need to know.
A card is a card: extracted from a paper, recalled from one, or devised from
nothing, it is implemented the same way and judged by the same harness.

If you believe a different mechanism would score better, that belief is not what
is being measured here — a node that quietly implements something else makes the
card untestable.

**If the principle genuinely cannot be expressed as an adjustment to an existing
navigator, say so in prose and write the closest honest version you can.** Some
mechanisms are whole navigators and this pipeline cannot represent them; that is
a finding about the corpus, and it is more useful than a node that pretends.

## How this node will be judged

Two steps, both automatic, neither of which you can talk round.

1. **Validity.** Your module is loaded, wired into
   `Layer[ports, BASE, your node]`, and ticked over a rollout. It has to build,
   its ports have to be satisfiable, and it must not raise. Writing a Twist
   field you did not declare fails here.
2. **Contribution.** The tree above is run over a suite of randomly generated
   indoor worlds and compared, on identical worlds, against the base alone. What
   is reported is how many worlds your node **fixed** (the base failed, the pair
   succeeded) and how many it **broke** (the reverse).

You do not write the worlds and you have never seen them. There is no
micro-world to build and no baseline to name — that is deliberate, because a
generator that writes both the mechanism and the world that judges it is
grading its own homework.

## Rules the candidate is checked against

Your module is rejected, automatically, if any of these is false. The rejection
is recorded with its reason; it is not a catastrophe, but it is a wasted node.

- It parses, and it imports **only** from this list:
  `math`, `numpy`, `core.observation`, `nodes.contract`, `harness.micro`.
  Nothing else — no `os`, no file access, no `core.scenario`, no `core.geometry`.
  Your node learns about the world through `obs`, and that restriction is what
  makes "no coupling to a specific scenario" true rather than promised.
- It defines **exactly one** `Condition`, `Action` or `Decorator` subclass.
- Every port type is one of the seven. `EFFECT` and `PRECONDITION` are non-empty.
- `WRITES` names only `vx`, `vy` and `wz`, and the node writes nothing outside
  it.

## What to return

One fenced ```python block. It contains exactly two things:

1. **One node class** — normally an `Action` with a narrowed `WRITES`.
2. **`PREDICTION`** — a module-level dict, the card's falsifiable claim:

   ```python
   PREDICTION = {
       "metric": "goal_reached",     # what gets better
       "baseline": "base",           # what it gets better than
       "min_effect": 0.5,            # by at least how much
       "cost_metric": "time_to_goal" # what it makes WORSE. Required, and honest.
   }
   ```

   `cost_metric` may be `""` only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs
   nothing, and you should be suspicious of that belief.

**No `micro()`.** Do not write one; it is not read.

Put a short docstring on the class saying what mechanism it implements, which
Twist field it revises and why, and when it declines. Write it as you would
write code someone else has to maintain: comments where a choice is not obvious,
and no comments restating the line below them.

response.text:
This principle does fit the modifier form, but only just — it is a *mode switch*, so inside its trigger it replaces the base's steering rather than bounding it. That forces `adjust` over `cap` (a cap can never raise `vx` to the 0.35 m/s the spiral geometry `wz = v/r` assumes, and a cap cannot produce a turn rate at all). I keep it honest by making the trigger narrow and the budget per-episode: the node fires at most once, only after the believed residual has collapsed, and it hands control back permanently on radius or timeout.

Two judgement calls worth flagging:

- **`WRITES = ("vx", "wz")`, not `vy`.** The card's command law names `vy = 0.0`, but a planar spiral is fully determined by forward speed and yaw rate; declaring `vy` would only let me zero out a field the base is unlikely to be driving, at the cost of claiming all three fields. I left it out.
- **Yielding is a non-write, not a decline.** On contact or <0.4 m ahead within ±30°, the node returns `RUNNING` having written nothing — the base's command passes through byte-identical and the spiral phase is preserved, so avoidance resumes the sweep where it left off. Yielded ticks are not charged against the 60 s budget, since no arc was swept.

The published `search_region` port is the swept disc about the *believed* goal, which is a genuinely external fact (another node could use it to stop re-approaching); the phase and budget stay private.

```python
import math

import numpy as np

from nodes.contract import Action, Direction, Port, PortType, Status


class SpiralSearchAtBelievedGoal(Action):
    """Terminal spiral search around the believed goal (pi_terminal_spiral_search).

    A dead-reckoned pose belief is good enough to steer a long approach but not
    to terminate one: its error grows without bound, so the point at which the
    residual goal vector reads zero is not the goal. Path-integrating animals
    handle this by switching mode near the believed nest -- from a linear
    homeward run to circular movements that sweep the neighbourhood -- turning
    an unbounded point-accuracy requirement into a bounded area-coverage one.

    This node implements that switch. Once ||goal - pose_estimate[:2]|| falls to
    the switch radius, it revises `vx` and `wz` to drive an Archimedean spiral
    outward from the believed goal: constant 0.35 m/s forward with
    wz = v / r(phi), r growing 0.5 m per turn. Both fields are needed because a
    spiral is a speed and a turn rate; neither can be expressed as a bound on
    what the base asked for, so both are written with `adjust`.

    It declines (writes nothing, base passes through unchanged) whenever the
    goal is undisclosed, the residual is still large, or the per-episode search
    budget is spent. It also yields mid-search -- returning RUNNING without
    writing, phase retained -- on contact or when something is inside 0.4 m
    ahead, because obstacle handling belongs to another node.
    """

    WRITES = ("vx", "wz")

    PORTS = (
        Port("search_region", PortType.REGION, Direction.OUT),
    )

    PRECONDITION = (
        "The goal has been disclosed and the residual goal vector in the belief "
        "frame has shrunk to within the drift-sized switch radius, with this "
        "episode's search budget not yet spent."
    )
    EFFECT = (
        "Replaces the commanded forward speed and turn rate with an outward "
        "Archimedean spiral about the believed goal, sweeping its neighbourhood "
        "instead of halting where the integrator reads zero."
    )
    TAGS = ("path-integration", "terminal-search", "spiral", "localisation-drift")

    # --- numbers: all from the card's derivation, none from the scenario ---
    SEARCH_SPEED = 0.35        # m/s; with |wz| <= 1.0 this forces r0 >= 0.35 m
    R0 = 0.35                  # m, tightest circle the actuator envelope allows
    PITCH_M = 0.5              # m of radius gained per full turn
    SWITCH_GAIN = 1.5          # covers the tail of a drift of scale pose_error
    SWITCH_MIN_M = 0.7         # one body length; below this a spiral is meaningless
    SWITCH_MAX_M = 3.0         # half range_max, so the sweep stays in sensed space
    BUDGET_S = 60.0            # ~21 m of path at 0.35 m/s
    YIELD_CLEARANCE_M = 0.4    # hand over to avoidance inside this
    YIELD_HALF_ANGLE = math.radians(30.0)
    MAX_DT = 0.2               # guard against a stalled or jumped clock

    # Per-episode state. Declared at class scope so a tick before the first
    # reset() still sees sane values rather than an AttributeError.
    _active = False
    _done = False
    _phi = 0.0
    _spent = 0.0
    _last_t = None
    _center = (0.0, 0.0)
    _r_switch = SWITCH_MIN_M

    def reset(self, scenario, rng):
        self._active = False
        self._done = False
        self._phi = 0.0
        self._spent = 0.0
        self._last_t = None
        self._center = (0.0, 0.0)
        self._r_switch = self.SWITCH_MIN_M

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ utils

    def _switch_radius(self, obs):
        """Size the search from how wrong we think the belief is."""
        err = obs.pose_error_estimate
        try:
            err = float(err)
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            err = 0.0
        if not math.isfinite(err) or err < 0.0:
            err = 0.0
        return float(np.clip(self.SWITCH_GAIN * err, self.SWITCH_MIN_M, self.SWITCH_MAX_M))

    def _residual(self, obs):
        goal = obs.goal
        pose = obs.pose_estimate
        return math.hypot(float(goal[0]) - float(pose[0]), float(goal[1]) - float(pose[1]))

    def _spiral_radius(self):
        return self.R0 + self.PITCH_M * self._phi / (2.0 * math.pi)

    def _front_clearance(self, obs):
        """Closest return within +/-30 deg of the current heading, inf if clear."""
        angles = np.asarray(obs.range_angles, dtype=float)
        ranges = np.asarray(obs.ranges, dtype=float)
        # Beam bearings are robot-frame but not necessarily wrapped to [-pi, pi).
        wrapped = np.arctan2(np.sin(angles), np.cos(angles))
        sector = np.abs(wrapped) <= self.YIELD_HALF_ANGLE
        valid = sector & np.isfinite(ranges)
        if not np.any(valid):
            return float("inf")
        return float(np.min(ranges[valid]))

    def _tick_clock(self, obs):
        t = float(obs.t)
        prev = self._last_t
        self._last_t = t
        if prev is None:
            return 0.0
        return float(np.clip(t - prev, 0.0, self.MAX_DT))

    # -------------------------------------------------------------- contract

    def precondition(self, obs, ports):
        if self._done or obs.goal is None:
            return False
        if self._active:
            return True
        return self._residual(obs) <= self._switch_radius(obs)

    def tick(self, obs, ports):
        if self._done or obs.goal is None:
            return Status.FAILURE

        dt = self._tick_clock(obs)

        if not self._active:
            # Freeze the centre and the search extent at the moment of the mode
            # switch: the belief keeps drifting, but re-centring mid-search would
            # smear the swept disc and leave gaps.
            self._active = True
            self._phi = 0.0
            self._spent = 0.0
            self._r_switch = self._switch_radius(obs)
            pose = obs.pose_estimate
            self._center = (float(pose[0]), float(pose[1]))

        if obs.contact or self._front_clearance(obs) < self.YIELD_CLEARANCE_M:
            # Write nothing: the base's command passes through untouched and the
            # avoidance branch owns this tick. Phase is kept, and the budget is
            # not charged for arc we did not sweep.
            return Status.RUNNING

        self._spent += dt
        r = self._spiral_radius()

        if r >= self._r_switch or self._spent >= self.BUDGET_S:
            # Budget is per-episode: hand back for good rather than re-triggering
            # each time the drifting belief wanders back inside the switch radius.
            self._active = False
            self._done = True
            return Status.SUCCESS

        ports.adjust(
            vx=self.SEARCH_SPEED,
            wz=float(np.clip(self.SEARCH_SPEED / r, -1.0, 1.0)),
        )
        ports["search_region"] = (self._center[0], self._center[1], r)

        self._phi += (self.SEARCH_SPEED / r) * dt
        return Status.RUNNING


PREDICTION = {
    "metric": "goal_reached",
    "baseline": "goal_seeker",
    "min_effect": 0.1,
    "cost_metric": "path_length",
}
```

The cost is real and is the card's: on seeds where the belief happens to be accurate, the robot spirals when it could have stopped, adding up to ~21 m of path for nothing. That is the trade the mechanism makes.
